page.title: Security is fun: 10 cybersecurity practices every developer should know
page.description: A developer-focused checklist for building safer applications, from authentication to dependency management.

text.content: Security has a reputation for being scary, boring, or something you deal with later when the app is “more real.”

rich_text.plain_text: Security has a reputation for being scary, boring, or something you deal with later when the app is “more real.”

text.content: That is how you end up with production secrets in GitHub, admin endpoints protected by spirits, and a database full of plain-text passwords. Spooky stuff.

rich_text.plain_text: That is how you end up with production secrets in GitHub, admin endpoints protected by spirits, and a database full of plain-text passwords. Spooky stuff.

text.content: The good news is that basic security is not mysterious. Most of it comes down to a handful of habits: do not trust user input, do not leak secrets, do not invent your own authentication system, and do not assume nobody will find the weird endpoint you forgot about.

rich_text.plain_text: The good news is that basic security is not mysterious. Most of it comes down to a handful of habits: do not trust user input, do not leak secrets, do not invent your own authentication system, and do not assume nobody will find the weird endpoint you forgot about.

text.content: Here are ten practical security habits every developer should build into their workflow.

text.content: 1. Treat Every API Endpoint Like Someone Will Poke It

rich_text.plain_text: 1. Treat Every API Endpoint Like Someone Will Poke It

text.content: APIs are easy to forget about because users usually interact with your nice little frontend. Attackers do not care about your nice little frontend. They will call your endpoints directly.

rich_text.plain_text: APIs are easy to forget about because users usually interact with your nice little frontend. Attackers do not care about your nice little frontend. They will call your endpoints directly.

text.content: Every API route should answer a few basic questions:

rich_text.plain_text: Every API route should answer a few basic questions:

text.content: Who is making this request?

rich_text.plain_text: Who is making this request?

text.content: Are they allowed to do this?

rich_text.plain_text: Are they allowed to do this?

text.content: Is the input valid?

rich_text.plain_text: Is the input valid?

text.content: Could this endpoint be abused if someone called it 10,000 times?

rich_text.plain_text: Could this endpoint be abused if someone called it 10,000 times?

text.content: At minimum, use HTTPS, require authentication where needed, check authorization on sensitive actions, validate all input on the server, and rate-limit endpoints that can be spammed.

rich_text.plain_text: At minimum, use HTTPS, require authentication where needed, check authorization on sensitive actions, validate all input on the server, and rate-limit endpoints that can be spammed.

text.content: Also, never hardcode API keys or tokens in your source code. Secrets in Git have a special talent for becoming everyone’s secrets.

text.content: Authentication and authorization sound similar, but they solve different problems.

text.content: For authentication, do not casually roll your own system. Use a trusted provider like Clerk, Auth0, Supabase Auth, Firebase Auth, AWS Cognito, or a similar service unless you have a strong reason not to.

text.content: Authentication looks simple until you remember password resets, email verification, session expiry, MFA, OAuth edge cases, account recovery, bot protection, and breach handling. That is a lot of dragons for one login form.

text.content: Also worth knowing: OAuth 2.0 is mainly for authorization. If you need user identity, you usually want OpenID Connect on top of OAuth.

text.content: For data that needs to be decrypted later, such as API keys, access tokens, or sensitive user fields, use proper encryption. AES is a common standard, but the algorithm is only one part of the problem. The harder part is key management.

text.content: 4. Validate Input on the Server

rich_text.plain_text: 4. Validate Input on the Server

text.content: Client-side validation is great for user experience. It is not security.

rich_text.plain_text: Client-side validation is great for user experience. It is not security.

text.content: Final Thoughts

rich_text.plain_text: Final Thoughts

text.content: Security does not need to be dramatic. Most of it is not about wearing a hoodie in a dark room while reading assembly code.

rich_text.plain_text: Security does not need to be dramatic. Most of it is not about wearing a hoodie in a dark room while reading assembly code.

text.content: It is about consistent habits.

text.content: Validate input. Check authorization. Hash passwords. Protect secrets. Use HTTPS. Keep dependencies fresh. Watch your logs. Avoid building authentication from scratch unless you really know what you are signing up for.
